comment: Examples for the documentation playground. Every entry is verified by tools/check-examples.sh.

handshake.vcd.title: Ready/valid handshake
handshake.vcd.description: A byte stream across a ready/valid interface, with stalls and idle gaps. Scope dut, signals clk, data[7:0], valid, ready.

counter.vcd.title: Free running counter
counter.vcd.description: An 8 bit counter with a carry pulse every 16 ticks. Scope cpu, signals clk, count[7:0], carry.

fabric.vcd.title: Three handshake interfaces
fabric.vcd.description: One scope, top, with three ready/valid ports sharing a naming convention: in_, out_ and cmd_, each with valid, ready and data[7:0]. Shaped so that `groups` has something to find.

examples.title: Arithmetic and variables
examples.blurb: WAL is an S-expression language. Operators come first, and define binds a name.

examples.title: Functions and lists
examples.blurb: lambda makes a function, and map, filter and sort work over lists.

examples.title: What is in this waveform
examples.blurb: A dot joins the hierarchy, so dut.data is data inside module dut. A ^ prefix names a trace when several are loaded.

examples.title: Values at the current time
examples.blurb: get-signal reads a signal where the trace is positioned, and step moves it.

examples.title: Find the interfaces, then measure them all
examples.blurb: groups asks a structural question: which name prefixes have every suffix you name? Nothing is hardcoded, so in-groups then runs one expression against each interface it found and gives you an answer per group. #valid resolves against the current group, CG is the group itself.

examples.title: Work inside one level of the hierarchy
examples.blurb: A scope is a level of the design rather than a name prefix. Inside in-scope, CS is the scope, LOCAL-SIGNALS is what sits directly in it, and ~name reads a signal relative to it.

examples.title: Pull a field out of a bus
examples.blurb: slice reads a bit field, upper bit first and inclusive, the way hardware is written. At index 62 the counter holds 31, so the bits are 00011111: the high nibble is 1 and the low nibble is 15. With one index it reads a single bit. This is how an opcode or an address range gets decoded without arithmetic.

examples.title: Step forward without losing your place
examples.blurb: timeframe records where every trace is, runs the body, and puts the cursor back. That is what overlapping transactions need: step forward to find the end of one, then resume from where it started to find the next.

examples.title: Build a histogram while sweeping
examples.blurb: An array is a string-keyed map, and geta/default is what makes it an accumulator: geta raises on a missing key, so counting without a default means checking first. mapa turns the result into a list of pairs to print.

examples.title: Hamming weight over time
examples.blurb: How many bits are high in the whole scope, at every timestamp. The result is a list of (time value) pairs, so the viewer can mark it.

examples.title: Bits that toggled
examples.blurb: Hamming distance between consecutive timestamps, which is the switching activity that drives dynamic power.

examples.title: Statistics over the activity
examples.blurb: The pairs are ordinary lists, so pull out the values with map and summarise them.

examples.title: Distribution of the activity
examples.blurb: Most timestamps toggle a single bit, and the carries show up as the tail.

examples.title: Find the hot spots, mark them
examples.blurb: Keep only the timestamps where more than four bits toggled. The result is (time value) pairs, so Send to viewer drops a marker on each one.

examples.title: Busiest beats of the handshake
examples.blurb: The same idea on the handshake trace: the payload changes stand out against the clock toggling on its own.
